data.title: What Science and Religion Each Investigate
data.sourcePassage: Science is a method for investigating the natural world through observation, hypothesis, testing, evidence, and peer review. In science, the word 'theory' does not mean a guess — it means a well-tested, evidence-based explanation. The theory of evolution and the Big Bang theory are among the most strongly supported ideas in all of science. Science is excellent at answering 'how' questions: How did the universe form? How do species change? How do diseases spread? But science does not have the tools to answer 'ultimate questions' — questions like: Why is there something rather than nothing? Does life have a purpose? Is there a God? These questions belong to religious and philosophical inquiry. Religion investigates meaning, value, ultimate reality, and ethics. A key insight is that science and religion are largely asking different types of questions. This does not mean they never interact, but it does mean that simply assuming science 'disproves' religion misunderstands what both are doing.

data.title: The Big Bang, Evolution, and Religious Responses
data.sourcePassage: The Big Bang theory is the leading scientific explanation for the origin of the universe: approximately 13.8 billion years ago, all matter and energy expanded rapidly from an extremely hot, dense point. Evidence includes the observed expansion of galaxies and cosmic microwave background radiation. Evolution by natural selection is the scientific theory that all life on Earth shares common ancestors and diversified over millions of years; individuals with advantageous traits are more likely to survive and reproduce. Evidence includes the fossil record, DNA analysis, and comparative anatomy. Most mainstream religious traditions do not see these theories as incompatible with faith. Many Christians, Muslims, and Jews hold a position called theistic evolution — believing that evolution was the mechanism God used to create life. They argue that Genesis, read symbolically, conveys theological truths about who created and why, not a scientific account of how or when. A minority, including Young Earth Creationists, read Genesis literally and reject scientific timescales. Humanists and atheists accept these theories as complete explanations without requiring a creator.

data.title: Literal and Symbolic Interpretation
data.sourcePassage: One of the most important factors in whether a religious believer sees science and religion as compatible or in conflict is how they interpret their sacred texts. A literal interpretation reads the text as factually true exactly as written — every word is a historical or scientific claim. Someone who reads Genesis literally will hold that creation happened in six actual 24-hour days and that the Earth is around 6,000 years old. A symbolic or allegorical interpretation reads the text as conveying deeper theological truths through metaphor, poetry, or story. A symbolic reader of Genesis might say: the 'six days' express that creation is ordered and good; the point is who created (God) and why (love, goodness), not a scientific timetable. Most mainstream Christian, Jewish, and Muslim scholars favour symbolic or allegorical readings, and see no conflict between their faith and scientific findings. Neither approach is 'less religious' than the other — they represent different views about the nature and purpose of scripture. In Religious Studies, students should understand both positions fairly rather than assuming one is obviously correct.
